claims_guardrails: No source, no verdict: every figure traces to sources/ and is reconciled in FACT-CHECK.md.
The catch: Dr. Gultepe flagged Ch23 Chemotherapy as under-connected (required only Ch1; depends on core biology like metabolism and TME).
Framework: a named failure mode - the recall problem / precision-recall trade-off in automatic prerequisite extraction (Pan 2017; Liang 2015/2018) + a generality bias.

Diagnosis: NOT the redundancy cleanup (Ch23 required only Ch1 pre-reduction; no Metabolism/TME at any tier). Not 'fewer later' (avg 1.82 early vs 1.67 late). Two failures: mis-tiering + missing edges.

The chart (prereq_gap_data.csv): required cross-chapter prereqs per chapter; 13 of the 19 applied chapters (Ch20-38) have 0-1; the 5 disease chapters + Clinical Trials require nothing cross-chapter. [Corrected from the docs' '11 of 21'; see FACT-CHECK.md.]
Why: chunked authoring; over-strict required tier; lexical-vs-conceptual matching; integrative applied chapters.

Method: derive prereqs from the textbook's own concept/mechanism tags (1,340 sections); for each concept, credit its home chapter (concentration peak) weighted by specificity. Content-grounded, reviewable, reproducible.

Three iterations + a fix: v1 raw overlap (reproduced generality bias; Metabolism absent); v2 specificity filter (recovered Metabolism, dropped TME - tags over-labeled TME onto ~34/38 chapters); v3 concentration-home (recovered the real mechanisms); then restrict candidate homes to the foundational half (Ch1-19) to kill sibling contamination (a treatment is not a prereq of another treatment). Plus curricular rules R1 (treatment->Ch20), R2 (disease->Ch17).

Result: 146 proposals = 127 ADD + 10 PROMOTE + 9 exists (verified in the CSV). The 13 under-connected applied chapters drop to 0. Ch23 recovers Metabolism (Ch11) as required (ADD) and promotes Principles of Therapy (Ch20) to required.
Prevention: check_prereq_coverage.py flags applied chapters with <2 required cross-chapter prereqs; 25 issues on the current graph; gates the build.

HONEST BOUNDARY: a PROPOSAL, not approved (approve blank; needs_review=yes); faculty set the required tier. The content signal has recall gaps - e.g. the TME, which the reviewer expected for Chemotherapy, did not clear the automated bar. No learning-outcome claim.

beats.narration_text: Hello, fellows. Last week we shipped the three-tier prerequisites, and Dr. Gultepe reviewed them. She caught something: Chemotherapy, chapter twenty-three, required almost nothing, even though understanding it depends on core cancer biology, things like metabolism and the tumor microenvironment. And she said it wasn't isolated. So I treated her catch as a failure analysis: what systematically went wrong, why, and how to fix it so it can't quietly come back. The question: when your prerequisite extractor is precise but thin, how do you recover the links it missed, without just reproducing the bias that lost them?

beats.narration_text: First, the good news: this is a named, measured failure mode, not a mystery. In automatic prerequisite extraction there's a precision-recall trade-off, and my draft sat in the high-precision, low-recall corner. It caught the obvious links and missed the real ones. Paired with it is a generality bias: methods that lean on surface similarity reward broad, ubiquitous concepts over the specific mechanism a chapter actually depends on. Pan and Liang's work names both. So the fix isn't to try harder by hand, it's to attack recall directly.

beats.narration_text: The diagnosis. First, I ruled out the obvious suspect: last month's redundancy cleanup did not cause this. Even before it, chapter twenty-three required only chapter one, and never linked to metabolism or the tumor microenvironment at any tier. And it's not simply that later chapters have fewer prerequisites; the average is about the same, one point eight early versus one point seven late. It's two specific failures, concentrated in the applied chapters: mis-tiering, where real dependencies are present but demoted below required, and missing edges, where they're absent entirely.

beats.narration_text: Here's the shape of it. This is the number of required cross-chapter prerequisites per chapter. The foundational chapters, on the left, mostly clear the bar of two. But the applied chapters, the treatments and diseases, collapse: thirteen of them have zero or one required cross-chapter prerequisite. The five disease chapters and clinical trials require nothing from another chapter at all. That's the recall gap, made visible.

beats.narration_text: Four things caused it. The graph was drafted in chunks, chapter-range by chapter-range, so no single pass ever asked, across the whole book, what a treatment depends on. The required tier was kept deliberately strict, and for applied chapters that strictness demoted real dependencies. Applied chapters speak clinical language while mechanism chapters speak biology, so surface similarity is low even when the dependency is strong. And applied chapters are integrative, resting on many mechanisms at once, which is the single hardest case for a local, lexical method.

beats.narration_text: So instead of asserting the links, I derived them from the textbook's own content. Every section is tagged with the concepts and mechanisms it uses, across one thousand three hundred forty sections. For each concept an applied chapter relies on, I find its home, the earlier chapter that owns the most of it, and credit that chapter, weighted by how specific the concept is. Dependencies come out of the material itself, not my opinion, which makes every proposal reviewable and reproducible.

beats.narration_text: Getting a useful signal took three tries and a fix. Version one, raw concept overlap, just reproduced the generality bias, the top matches were ubiquitous concepts, and metabolism never showed up. Version two filtered for specificity, and recovered metabolism, but dropped the tumor microenvironment, because the tags had over-labeled it onto nearly every chapter. Version three, crediting each concept's home chapter, finally recovered the real mechanisms. Then one more fix: restrict candidates to the foundational half of the book, so a treatment doesn't come out as a prerequisite of another treatment.

beats.narration_text: The result is a hundred forty-six proposals: a hundred twenty-seven new links, ten promotions, and nine already correct. The thirteen under-connected applied chapters drop to zero. For chemotherapy specifically, it recovers metabolism as a required prerequisite, and promotes principles of therapy to required, exactly the kind of link the review was pointing at. And nothing is auto-applied; it's a reviewable proposal, with an approve column, and not a single edge is written until it's confirmed.

beats.narration_text: Two last things, and an honest limit. To stop this recurring, a coverage check flags any applied chapter with fewer than two required cross-chapter prerequisites; it finds twenty-five issues on the current graph and can gate the build, so under-connection is caught automatically instead of in review. But this is a proposal, not an approved change: every row is marked needs-review, and faculty set the required tier. And the content signal still has gaps; a dependency a reviewer expects, like the tumor microenvironment for chemotherapy, can still fall below the automated bar. That's precisely why the expert, not the tool, has the final say.
